Consideration of the needs of endangered species and subspecies suggest that water development projects which threaten the welfare of these animals may have to be altered, dropped, postponed, or moved to a more costly site if restoration of the species is to be successful. These projects will include impoundments for the storage of water for power production, irrigation, navigation, flood control, recreation, or municipal, industrial, and domestic use. They may include construction of canals for the transport of water or navigation and the extraction of ground water for irrigation of agricultural crops.
Economic impacts will sometimes occur in the form of loss of benefits of water development foregone, cost of relocation of a project to an alternative site, or modification of the development project to mitigate the damage to an endangered animal.
is illustrated by the following examples. Impoundments may inundate the habitat of stream fishes such as has happened to the trispot and Tuscumbia darters in Alabama. Several forms of land snails in California are threatened by inundation of their habitat by impoundments. Dams may block the access of anadromous fishes to their spawning sites. The Devil's Hole pupfish and several other desert fishes are threatened by massive extractions of ground water for irrigation of surrounding desert lands. Water in the endemic spring threatens to fall below tolerable levels unless pumping is curtailed.
